title: Throw away the thirst for books
word: Throw away the thirst for books
hookLine: stop craving more books, and die content, not grumbling (Meditations 2.3)

lines: THROW AWAY THE THIRST FOR BOOKS.
cards: The pile by the bed. The library holds. The audiobooks at one and a half speed.

The saved articles you'll get to someday. For a lot of curious people, the next book is a kind of hunger that never quite ends. Now, in the third entry of book two, Marcus says something odd for a man who loved reading.

teach.h: LET THESE BE ENOUGH FOR YOU.
teach.b: First, what comes before it. Section three is a quick sketch of how Marcus sees the world: everything from the gods is full of providence, everything hangs together, and what serves the whole is good for each part.
Let these be enough for you, he tells himself; hold them as settled. Second, the line.
And throw away the thirst for books, he says, so that you don't die grumbling, but cheerful, truthful, and thankful to the gods from the heart.
Third, the word thirst. He doesn't say throw away books. This is a man who thanked Rusticus for lending him Epictetus and thanked his great-grandfather for good teachers.

teach.h: READ A FEW; LIVE BY THEM.
teach.b: It's thirst: the feeling that the answer is always in the next book, so you never have to live by the ones you've read.
Seneca said the same in his second letter, read on this path this year: a mind that's everywhere is nowhere. Fourth, why it matters at the end. Marcus ties this to dying content.

Picture someone at the end of life still anxious about all the books they never got to. Now picture someone who read a few, lived by them, and could say thank you. That second ending is the one he wants.

There's a gentle joke in today, too: a daily path built on reading, telling you to put a book down. But that's the point of a daily path. One small thing, practiced, instead of a hundred things collected.

how: Some readers of Marcus limit how much new reading they take on and spend more time rereading and practicing a few texts they trust.

games.q: what does “throw away the thirst for books” mean?
o: let go of craving the next book; live what you've read
burn the books of rival schools so only one remains
stop reading entirely, since books only distract the mind

games.q: throw away the thirst for books — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus tells himself to stop reading altogether
he says throw away the thirst for books, not books themselves.
Marcus ties the thirst for books to how he wants to die
not grumbling, but cheerful, truthful and thankful.
this line contradicts Marcus's thanks to Rusticus for lending him Epictetus
reading isn't the problem; endless craving instead of living is.

games.q: you've finished a book that changed how you see things. what does Meditations 2.3 suggest you do next?
o: live by what you just read, and let it be enough for now.
games.why: let these principles be enough, he says, and throw away the thirst for books.

practice: Picture your own pile, the books, the podcasts, the saved articles, and feel the small tug of it. Now pick one thing you've already read or heard that's genuinely worth living by, a line, a story, a rule, and hold it.
If it were enough for today, what would you do with it?

wordCard.voice: Throw away the thirst for books. Not the books, the thirst, so that you live by what you've read and end your days thankful, not grumbling. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: thirst. Marcus throws away the thirst for books, not the books.

carryVoice: Your line: enough reading. Enough isn't none; it's enough to live on. Day five hundred thirty-two, the end of a week.
